text: September 2007. Johannesburg. The first-ever T20 World Cup final. India against Pakistan. Pakistan need thirteen runs off the last six balls.
And the captain, twenty-six-year-old M S Dhoni, hands the ball not to his experienced spinner, but to Joginder Sharma, a medium-pacer with just seven international matches behind him.
Was that genius? Or did he just get lucky? The honest answer is one of the most important lessons in business, and every great CFO knows it.
A captain and a CFO have the same job: make big, often irreversible calls with incomplete information, while millions judge them afterwards.
Let's break down three real match decisions, and the three decision rules hidden inside them.
Rule one starts in Mumbai. April the second, twenty eleven. The World Cup final. India are chasing two hundred and seventy-five against Sri Lanka.
Virat Kohli falls at one hundred and fourteen for three. Yuvraj Singh, the player of the tournament, is the obvious next batter.
But out walks Dhoni himself, averaging only about thirty in the tournament so far.
Why? Muttiah Muralitharan was bowling, and Dhoni had faced Murali for years in the Chennai Super Kings nets. He could read him. Murali later said Yuvraj didn't have a clue against him.
Dhoni finished on ninety-one not out, off seventy-nine balls, and sealed the World Cup with a six.

In the boardroom, when a CFO approves an acquisition, the real question isn't, is this a good company? It's, do we know something the market doesn't? Warren Buffett calls it your circle of competence.
Rule one. Under uncertainty, bet where your information is better than everyone else's.
Rule two. November twenty twenty-three, Ahmedabad. Over ninety-two thousand fans. India have won all ten matches. Australia's captain, Pat Cummins, wins the toss.
And he chooses to bowl first, a call almost nobody expected in a final.
His logic had two layers. First, the conditions: a dry pitch he expected to get easier for batting under lights, once the dew arrived.

Second, and this is the CFO part, Cummins reportedly judged that getting it wrong with the bat first would be fatal, in a way that getting it wrong with the ball would not. He wasn't chasing the best average. He was cutting off the worst case.
India were bowled out for two hundred and forty. Travis Head made one hundred and thirty-seven. Australia won by six wickets.
Great CFOs think the same way. They give up some upside so that no single bad scenario can kill the company. More cash. Less debt. Investments made in stages.
Jeff Bezos called these one-way doors and two-way doors. If you can't walk back through the door, protect the downside first.
Rule two. Before you ask what's the best case, ask which mistake you cannot survive.
Now, back to Johannesburg. Thirteen off six. Why Joginder?

According to teammates, Dhoni believed overs seventeen to nineteen often matter more than the twentieth, so he spent his best bowlers there. That's resource allocation: putting capital where its impact is highest.
And in the seventeenth over, Misbah-ul-Haq had hit Harbhajan Singh for three sixes. Against a right-hander, Dhoni backed Joginder's pace.
Then it started going wrong. A wide. A dot ball. And then, Misbah hit a six. Six needed off four.
Next ball, Misbah tried a scoop. He mistimed it. Sreesanth held the catch at short fine leg. India won by five runs.
Here's the uncomfortable truth. If that scoop had cleared the fielder, the same decision, with the same logic, would be remembered as one of the worst calls in Indian cricket.

Former poker champion Annie Duke calls this mistake resulting: judging a decision only by its outcome. Her example is the Seattle Seahawks' pass call on the one-yard line in Super Bowl forty-nine. It was intercepted, and the coach was called an idiot overnight, though many analysts argued the call was defensible.
That's why the best finance teams keep decision journals: what they knew, the options and the odds, written down before the result arrives.
Rule three. Grade the process, not the scoreboard.
But careful. Trust the process can also become an excuse for ignoring obvious warning signs.
The fix is psychologist Gary Klein's pre-mortem. Before you commit, imagine the decision has already failed, and list every reason why.
So, genius or luck? It's the wrong question. Great captains and great CFOs bet where they have an edge, avoid the mistakes they can't survive, and judge themselves on process, not the scoreboard.
Which captaincy call do you think was pure genius, and which was just luck? Tell us in the comments.
